pages.title: What Is Waste?
pages.content:
By definition, waste refers to any unwanted matter or material, particularly what is left after useful parts are removed. In the context of zero waste, however, waste is not merely what is left over, but rather a direct consequence of poor product planning and unsustainable consumption patterns. The core idea of zero waste is to reduce waste production as much as possible.

Key statistics on waste highlight the importance of the issue:

Global municipal solid waste generation is predicted to grow from 2.3 billion tons in 2023 to 3.8 billion tons by 2050.

Around the world, only 62 percent of city waste is processed within proper waste management facilities.

Globally, food and other organic materials represent the largest portion of municipal solid waste, followed closely by paper, cardboard, and plastics. As economies expand, their waste patterns also shift. The rapid increase in plastic waste is particularly alarming, as huge amounts of it are ending up in oceans and rivers. However, municipal waste consists of various other materials, each requiring unique collection and recycling methods.

pages.title: Paper and Wood
pages.content:
Paper Waste: The natural source of paper is forests. Paper waste management is important because paper recycling saves a huge amount of raw materials and brings high economic value.

To prevent them from getting wet, paper materials are collected separately from other waste and are compressed for easier transportation. Paper waste is processed in recycling facilities using various methods to be transformed into new paper and cardboard products.

Wood Waste: Wood obtained from trees is widely used in daily life for household goods, packaging, and construction, serving as an essential material to transport and protect various products. Recycling centers apply various methods to transform wood waste into useful timber and boards, enabling these materials to be effectively reused instead of being disposed of as waste.

pages.title: Plastic
pages.content: Plastic Waste: Plastic is a core material in many consumer products and is found in a large share of manufactured goods. However, because different types of plastics exist, they cannot all be recycled in the same way. Between 2000 and 2019, global plastic production almost doubled, rising from 234 to 460 million tons (a 97 percent increase). Over the same period, plastic waste grew even faster, rising from 156 to 353 million tons (a 126 percent increase). Looking at the final stage of the plastic lifecycle, only 9 percent was recycled, 19 percent was burned in waste facilities, and 50 percent went to sanitary landfills. The remaining 22 percent was either left in uncontrolled dumps, burned in open pits, or leaked into the environment, mostly into waterways.

pages.title: Glass and Composite Packaging
pages.content:
Glass Waste: The main raw materials of glass are sand, soda ash, and limestone. Glass products, such as beverage bottles and jars, become glass waste at the end of their lifespan. Glass waste is collected in specialized containers and sorted by color to ensure high-quality, continuous recycling. These materials are then remelted in facilities to manufacture new packaging.

Composite Waste: Composite packaging, made by combining paperboard, plastic and, in many cases, a thin layer of aluminum, is widely used for juice and milk cartons. However, this also creates a massive amount of waste. Composite waste requires separate collection and processing in advanced facilities designed to break down the adhesive bonds between these layers. Once these materials are successfully sorted, they are recycled into secondary raw materials or used to produce new consumer goods.

pages.title: Metal and Vegetable Oil
pages.content:
Metal Waste: Metal is produced by processing and purifying different minerals found in the Earth. Aluminum beverage cans, oil and tomato paste cans are metal wastes. Metal waste must be collected separately for recovery. Once collected, these metals are melted down to manufacture new products.

Vegetable Waste Oil: Vegetable oil is the general term for oils made from oil-rich plant seeds, such as olives, sunflowers, corn, cotton, soybeans, canola, and safflower. Used frying oil, solid fats and oils past their expiration date are vegetable waste oil. Vegetable waste oil must be collected separately to protect water systems from pollution. This oil is then processed in specialized facilities to be transformed into clean, renewable biodiesel.

pages.title: Organic Waste
pages.content: Organic Waste: Organic materials play an important role in daily life and agricultural activities, resulting in both animal and plant-based waste. For instance, fruit and vegetable scraps, along with wheat, barley, and rye straw, are all classified as organic waste. Data shows that 13.2 percent of the world's food was lost post-harvest along the food chain before it reached the customer and an additional 17 percent is wasted at the house, hospitality, or retail level. 61 percent of food waste occurs in households.

pages.title: Electronic Waste and Batteries
pages.content:
Electronic Waste: Electronic devices are widely used in homes, schools, and offices, significantly facilitating our daily tasks. Discarded appliances such as dishwashers, washing machines, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, toasters, computers, and cell phones are all classified as electronic waste. Electronic waste must be collected in separate bins to ensure the safe removal of toxic substances. These discarded devices are then dismantled into smaller parts, allowing valuable materials like metals, plastics, and rare elements to be recovered.

Waste Batteries: Batteries are devices that store energy in chemical form and convert it directly into electrical energy. Once they reach the end of their lifespan or become unusable due to physical damage, they are classified as waste batteries. Waste batteries must be collected in dedicated bins to prevent hazardous chemicals from leaking into the soil and water. These batteries are then processed in specialized facilities to safely extract critical metals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel for reuse.

As we can see, while recycling processes successfully recover valuable materials, they still require significant energy and effort. So, recycling alone is not enough to solve the problem. This is where the concept of Zero Waste comes in, shifting our focus from simply managing waste to preventing it completely from the very beginning.

pages.title: What Is Zero Waste?
pages.content:
When you hear the phrase ‘zero waste’, you might think it means producing absolutely no refuse. But that’s just not possible! We all use products and create waste every single day. So, what does ‘zero waste’ actually mean?

Zero Waste is a sustainable approach focused on using resources smartly and minimizing waste. This approach is based on the core principle of sustainability, which means meeting our current needs without damaging the resources that future generations will need. Zero Waste approach encourages people to make and use things responsibly by avoiding waste, reusing items, and recycling. This mindset supports eco-friendly habits and invites us to look at the entire product lifecycle. In the end, this ensures nothing goes to waste, helping society see leftover materials as something valuable.

Every year, people generate between 2.1 and 2.3 billion tons of municipal waste. This means we are discarding valuable resources that could easily return to the economy and reduce the demand for new, raw materials. This ongoing pollution threatens our well-being, damages economies, and accelerates both climate change and biodiversity loss. In response to this global crisis, zero waste is recognized as an essential bridge to the circular economy.

pages.title: The Circular Economy
pages.content: The circular economy aims to eliminate waste and pollution by keeping products and materials in use for as long as possible. In simple terms, it works just like nature, where nothing is wasted and everything is reused over and over again. It is called 'circular' because instead of moving in a straight line from manufacturing to the landfill, resources move in a continuous loop, constantly turning old products into new ones. At its core, the main objective is to ensure economic growth no longer comes at the expense of nature. The circular economy is the exact opposite of the traditional linear economy, which follows a simple 'take-make-waste' model. In the linear system, the process goes only one way: resources are taken from nature, used, and then thrown away.

pages.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
pages.content:
The foundation of a zero waste vision is built on three main principles that are closely linked to the circular economy: Reduce, Reuse-Repair and Recycle-Upcycle.

Reduce: The principle of 'Reduce' focuses on preventing waste at the source by intentionally consuming fewer resources and buying only what is necessary.

Reuse and Repair: This principle addresses the concept of designing products for longevity so they can be used over and over again instead of being thrown away. It focuses on designing products and materials to last for as long as possible. To do this, products should be made more durable, easy to repair, and simple to upgrade. Repairing places emphasis on fixing broken or damaged items. Doing this helps extend the lifespan of products and saves money at the same time.

Recycle and Upcycle: The principle seeks to keep products and materials inside the economy for as long as possible. This can be achieved by collecting and recycling waste, or by designing products that are easy to take apart and reuse. Recycling involves converting waste into new materials and products. This process helps reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills and saves natural resources. Upcycling targets transforming waste into new products of higher value.

pages.title: Why Is the Circular Economy Important?
pages.content:
The circular economy offers several key benefits, including:

Reducing waste and pollution: First, the circular economy helps reduce the total amount of waste and pollution. By keeping products and materials in use for as long as possible, it lowers the need to take new resources from nature and manufacture new products.

Utilizing resources more efficiently: The circular economy centers on using resources more efficiently. This is achieved by minimizing the use of materials from the very beginning, while maximizing the reuse and recycling of waste.

Supporting sustainable economic growth: This approach supports sustainable economic growth. It works by lowering the costs of waste disposal and creating new jobs in the recycling and reuse industry.

The circular economy is a promising new way of thinking about economics. It has the potential to reduce waste, lower pollution, improve resource efficiency, and support sustainable economic growth. As we move toward a more sustainable future, the circular economy will play an increasingly important role.

pages.title: Waste and Climate
pages.content:
The way we manage our waste is directly linked to the global climate crisis, making 'Zero Waste' practices a powerful tool in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Greenhouse gases from waste significantly contribute to this crisis, especially because organic materials release potent methane when they rot in landfills. Due to unsustainable production and consumption habits, global greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled over the last 50 years. To stop this dangerous trend, adopting a Zero Waste approach is essential, as it keeps resources out of landfills and prevents these harmful emissions at the source.

Improving how we manage waste across the entire product lifecycle could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 15 to 20 percent. However, a major injustice exists: many developing countries have very low emission levels, yet they often suffer the most from climate impacts like severe disasters and rising sea levels.

Minimizing greenhouse gas emissions across the entire product lifecycle is vital to reducing the effects of climate change. Furthermore, sustainable waste management reduces short-lived air pollutants like methane and black carbon, which come from open dumping and burning. In the end, these efforts are crucial to protecting our atmosphere.

pages.title: How Can We Help?
pages.content:
The best kind of waste is the one that is never created at all. Therefore, taking action before waste is even generated is essential to prevent managing waste that should not exist. Here are a few practical approaches, examples of behavior and suggestions:

Food waste can be minimized through proper training, encouragement, and better buying policies in canteens, restaurants, hotels, hospitals, and households. Similarly, packaging-free shops and local markets can stop both packaging and food waste while offering fresh food. Most single-use packaging is actually unnecessary and can be easily replaced through local city actions. To-go coffee cups, take-away containers, disposable water bottles, and plastic straws are just a few items that can be swapped for waste-free alternatives.

pages.title: Cities, Families and the Future
pages.content:
Local governments can also play a major role by introducing refillable systems for drinks, reuse programs for diapers, and ensuring waste-free sanitary products are available in local stores. For long-lasting goods like electronics, furniture, or clothing, it is crucial to support repair and reuse through second-hand shops and reuse platforms, both offline and online. Additionally, cities can use the financial power of public purchasing to shift the market, encourage paperless offices, and set up tool libraries or material banks to prevent waste locally.

These options are simple to put into practice and are becoming increasingly available to all of us. Ultimately, educating and involving children along with their families is the most effective way to transform society's wasteful habits, and there is no better moment to act than now.

Since Zero Waste is a mindset rather than a physical result, achieving a waste-free society is not a final destination but an ongoing journey.

In a world obsessed with overconsumption, we must once again remind ourselves of Gandhi’s wise insight: “The world has enough for everyone's need, but not enough for everyone's greed.”
